Trend in a short series

Source: R/trend.R
trndtst.Rd

Tests whether a short series (for example five to ten fiscal years of an administrative count) is rising or falling, and estimates the size of the change per period. It uses the Mann-Kendall rank test for monotone trend and the Theil-Sen median-of-slopes estimator: no distributional assumption, resistant to a single aberrant period, and meaningful at the series lengths an annual administrative extract actually has.

Usage

trndtst(
  y,
  x = NULL,
  value = NULL,
  prd = NULL,
  exact = NULL,
  alt = c("two.sided", "increasing", "decreasing"),
  conflvl = 0.95
)

Arguments

y

Numeric vector, the series in period order, or a data frame.

x

Numeric vector of periods, default NULL: the position 1, 2, ..., which is right for an evenly spaced series. Ignored when y is a data frame and prd is given.

value, prd

Column names (strings), when y is a data frame. value is required; prd is optional and must be convertible with as.numeric().

exact

Logical or NULL (the default). Whether to compute the exact null distribution of Mann-Kendall's \(S\) by enumeration. NULL uses it up to n = 8 (40,320 orderings); above that the normal approximation with the tie and continuity corrections is used.

alt

"two.sided" (the default), "increasing" or "decreasing".

conflvl

Number in (0, 1), default 0.95: the confidence level of the slope interval.

Value

A list with S, tau, p_value, slope (Theil-Sen, in units of y per unit of x), intercept, slopelo and slopeup (the distribution-free interval), slopecicla (TRUE when the pairwise slopes do not reach the requested confidence on a side, so that bound is the extreme slope and the true interval is wider), n, var_S (the tie-corrected variance of \(S\)), alternative, conflvl and method.

Details

With values \(y_1, \dots, y_n\) in period order, $$S = \sum_{i < j} \mathrm{sign}(y_j - y_i),$$ and Kendall's tau here is \(S / (n(n-1)/2)\), the rank correlation between the value and the period. The Theil-Sen slope is the median of the pairwise slopes \((y_j - y_i)/(x_j - x_i)\); intercept is the line's intercept from the compiled Theil-Sen routine.

For \(n \le 8\) the p-value is exact by default: \(S\) is computed over every ordering of the observed values (with ties kept, so tied data get the correct conditional null). Otherwise the normal approximation is used, with the tie-corrected variance of \(S\) and a continuity correction of one unit toward zero. Exact tables are cached in the session, up to 32 of them. A series whose values are all tied has \(S = 0\) in every ordering, so its p-value is 1 at every length.

The slope interval is the standard rank-based one: the pairwise slopes are sorted and the interval runs between the order statistics that Mann-Kendall's variance places at the chosen level, so it is consistent with the test rather than derived from a different model. At small \(n\) the slopes may not reach the requested confidence; the bound is then the most extreme slope and slopecicla is TRUE.

Missing periods are dropped and the series is sorted by x. Errors: fewer than three periods; infinite values; x and y of different lengths; a period given twice in x; a data frame without value or with a column not found; more than 20,000 periods (the pairwise slopes would not fit in memory); a conflvl outside (0, 1). exact = TRUE with \(n > 8\) warns and uses the normal approximation.

References

Sen, P. K. (1968). Estimates of the regression coefficient based on Kendall's tau. Journal of the American Statistical Association 63(324), 1379-1389, for the median-of-slopes estimator and the distribution-free interval.

Wilcox, R. R. Modern Statistics for the Social and Behavioral Sciences: A Practical Introduction treats Theil-Sen among the regression methods that carry no normality assumption, which is the reason for preferring it on a series this short.

See also

stepchg, cnttrnd

Examples

# Five years of placements.
y <- c(402, 377, 190, 268, 331)
trndtst(y)
#> $S
#> [1] -4
#> 
#> $tau
#> [1] -0.4
#> 
#> $p_value
#> [1] 0.4833333
#> 
#> $slope
#> [1] -21.375
#> 
#> $intercept
#> [1] 419.75
#> 
#> $slopelo
#> [1] -187
#> 
#> $slopeup
#> [1] 78
#> 
#> $slopecicla
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $n
#> [1] 5
#> 
#> $var_S
#> [1] 16.66667
#> 
#> $alternative
#> [1] "two.sided"
#> 
#> $conflvl
#> [1] 0.95
#> 
#> $method
#> [1] "Mann-Kendall, exact over all 120 orderings"
#> 

# A monotone series is detected even at n = 5, where a regression's
# standard error would be nearly uninformative.
trndtst(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))
#> $S
#> [1] 10
#> 
#> $tau
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $p_value
#> [1] 0.01666667
#> 
#> $slope
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $intercept
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $slopelo
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $slopeup
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $slopecicla
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $n
#> [1] 5
#> 
#> $var_S
#> [1] 16.66667
#> 
#> $alternative
#> [1] "two.sided"
#> 
#> $conflvl
#> [1] 0.95
#> 
#> $method
#> [1] "Mann-Kendall, exact over all 120 orderings"
#> 

# One aberrant period does not create a trend.
trndtst(c(100, 100, 100, 100, 900))$p_value
#> [1] 0.4

# From a data frame, testing for a decrease only.
d <- data.frame(year = 2019:2023, n = y)
trndtst(d, value = "n", prd = "year", alt = "decreasing")$p_value
#> [1] 0.2416667

try(trndtst(c(5, 6)))
#> Error : trndtst: a trend needs at least three periods
